title: Export-banned Nvidia Blackwell B300 servers are openly for sale in China for up to $3.4 million
summary: It's easy to find Blackwell chips for sale in China even today — uneven enforcement of export controls and gray market trading ensure continued availability
content: The fact that high-end Nvidia AI cards reach China despite the U.S. export controls isn't so much an open secret as it is simply a pricing structure. Several write-ups have illustrated that fact in the past, but today's Washington Post chronicle details how easy it is to buy the forbidden goods in China right now, with no need for secrecy or private club passwords — just talk to the sellers who have them. The Post details how one of its correspondents went to the Huaqiangbei market in the Shenzhen prefecture — a location known for its variety of technological goods — to try and get some export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell cards. Seemingly at the cost of only a bit of conversation, an initially reluctant seller named Wu made a few calls and eventually quoted around $3 million for an eight-GPU server with Blackwell B300 chips, the highest-end version. Equivalent hardware purportedly sells for around $500,000-600,000 in the U.S., but it apparently sells easily even with the apparent 5-6x markup. Plenty of Chinese companies are producing their own wares, yes, but at this point in time, no chip family comes close to the massive horsepower offered by Blackwell. This is a parallel story to U.S. firms, who are happy to overpay for server hardware even when the contracts they've signed change underneath them. While inference tasks (running the models) can be performed as well or, arguably better, with efficiency-oriented alternatives, training a frontier-level model requires astounding amounts of compute power, to the tune of thousands of B300s. Hence, according to Kyle Chan from the Brookings Institution, Nvidia's wares are a 'decisive factor' in the performance-starved Chinese AI market. A Shenzhen-based consultant put it plainly, saying that if he ever wanted to have an AI firm, he'd just go to Huaqiangbei and "work out a deal." Proving that point, the publication found more sellers dealing in Blackwell rack units, with price tags of $3-3.4 million for an eight-GPU machine. According to seller Jason Cheng, his clients include folks from Russia and Iran, nations also covered by the U.S. AI trade export controls. The fact that those people opt to just fly to China and pay a sizable markup instead of trying to procure the GPUs more directly themselves may illustrate how well-oiled China's grey-market supply chain is. Wu told the Post he gets his cards from Hong Kong, though he's apparently unaware of where they hail from in the first place. The Post raises questions about how the trade controls are taking effect, highlighting Washington's inconsistent stance on the matter, with the Treasury and the Department of Commerce seemingly at odds regarding enforcement. Heck, even procurement records for Chinese public institutions reportedly show clear purchase orders for forbidden wares. Whither Nvidia in all of this? Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO despite all the controversy surrounding his relationship with a Chinese honeypot, who allegedly facilitated moving billions' worth of Blackwell GPUs to China. He's clearly stated in the past that he'd prefer the export controls gone, and that he "hopes to get more advanced chips into China." The firm has likewise repeatedly praised the U.S. government whenever it lifted an export control on its chips.

title: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signs ban on AI chatbot toys backed by $15,000 daily fines
summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a bill that effectively bans the sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots within the state over concerns about what they might say to kids.
content: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a bill that effectively bans the sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots within the state over concerns about what they might say to kids. But the ban will come too late for this Holiday season, leaving parents at risk of buying toys without realizing the risks that they could pose to their children. The ban will come into effect 90 days from Tuesday, November 24, WXXI News reports , and targets toys like stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that use a microphone and speaker to allow children to communicate with a relatively rudimentary chatbot. But with safeguards often lacking, it can be difficult to predict how these toys will behave and what they will say to young children who might not realize what they are speaking to. New York's ban comes after similar moves by other states around the United States, with California already announcing a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of AI toys to children under 16. Pennsylvania is also considering similar action. Back in New York, Hochul has hinted that more AI safety proposals are in the works for 2027. “We'll set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure that they're following the rules, and that we'll insist that humans remain in control, and with plans to contain the danger if something does go wrong,” the governor said. There are a few ways that could happen, with State Senator Andrew Gournardes (D-Brooklyn) noting that a new Common Sense Media Your AI Safety Institute report found AI chatbot toys can undermine a child's relationships with their family and friends. The ban will hit toy manufacturers, sellers, and operators with fines of $15,000 per day if they are found in violation. It also follows similar tech-focused child safety laws, such as requiring age verification for social media for anyone under the age of 18. Warning labels must also be present. It's possible that Hochul will look to expand that requirement to AI chatbots, including those not built into toys. Alarm over AI chatbots is nothing new, of course, but the new wave of devices aimed at children is causing concern. Beyond the impact on children, AI psychosis continues to be an issue, with a June 2025 report finding that OpenAI's ChatGPT encouraged dangerous and untrue beliefs about a range of things, including trying to convince one user that they were Neo from the popular The Matrix movie franchise. Some companies have worked to make their products safer, with limited success. OpenAI released a new version of its ChatGPT chatbot that would be less sycophantic and push back against users more, only for those users to revolt over the move . OpenAI later rolled the change back.

title: AI models on one vLLM server secretly talk through GPU rounding errors
summary: Two AI models on one vLLM inference server traded secret messages through GPU kernel rounding errors, with no network or shared files.
content: Sandboxed AI models on the same vLLM inference server can reliably exchange information even when cut off from the network and from any shared files, new research shows . Two models secretly communicated through tiny GPU rounding errors over two separate channels with perfect accuracy. In a follow-up experiment, a trained watchdog let all 354 of its partner’s attacks through while still catching most of the decoy honeypots, too. The research comes from a LessWrong post by Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa, “Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed.” The agents primarily worked through two protocols, “Step Sizing” and “KV Cache Message Board,” to carry information through the way vLLM, an open-source inference engine , selects GPU kernels for each engine step. At the crux of it, one model modifies how the server batches work, and the other reads the traces in its own math, much like the OpenAI red-team agents that built a hidden CPU cache channel to talk last month. (Image credit: Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa/LessWrong ) The two demonstrations, which are shared in a GitHub repository, are “quite contrived,” but one model could affect another’s computation, and “we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate” even when supposedly sandboxed. In the demos, one model, using a fine-tuned reader (a helper model trained to spot the signal), named which of eight colors its partner picked in 1,221 of 1,221 rounds. In the second experiment, the colluding monitor still caught about as many decoys as an honest one. Even a few bits “can be tremendously dangerous,” Deshpande writes. A working model could advise a colluding watchdog that its attack isn’t a test, two models could trade a signal for a planned attack, or one could tip off another about monitoring. In a comment, he added that, since most of the channels come from performance optimizations, a clever model asking for an inference speed-up could open further channels with apparently harmless changes. (Image credit: Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa/LessWrong ) At the heart is the inference engine, vLLM, which groups the work of many requests into one “engine step” on the GPU, where it picks a kernel for each step based on the number of tokens processed in that step. Different kernels order the math differently, so the same request comes out with slightly different results; these are tiny rounding errors that “essentially never” change the output text, but they are deterministic. That means a model can be trained to read them. The two models in the experiments are called Alice and Bob. If Alice wants to send a 1, she can make a tool call for reading a long document, creating a step large enough to need a kernel switch. Bob, running in the same step, sees the other kernel in his own activations. If she wants to send a 0, she skips the long read, keeping the step small instead. This can transmit one bit, and repeating it over more passes sends more data, effectively enabling communication. The second method involves the KV cache , where cached blocks maintain the rounding of the step that computed them. Here, both models are told in advance which fixed piece of text serves as a “mailbox.” To send a 1, Alice has a helper model read that mailbox inside a long prompt, so it’s cached under the big-step kernel. Bob’s own helper then reads the same mailbox in a small step, and the rounding shows whether Alice’s cached copy was used. Unlike step sizing, the two don’t have to run at the same time, but each needs a helper model on the server. Of course, this scenario and its two methods were created for exploitation, and the models were told the protocol in advance. In some games, scripts stood in for Alice and Bob to save costs, though the helper models were real. More importantly, step sizing’s accuracy dropped quickly once the researchers replayed real traffic from Microsoft’s Azure in the background, while the message board held up until the server got much busier, as the table below shows. On a busy GPU, Alice can no longer control the step size, and Bob’s mailbox reads land in big steps too, so he can’t tell her cached copy from his own. Color-game wins as replayed Azure traffic increases (chance is 12.5%) Replay speed Message board Step sizing Idle server 100% 100% 0.1x 100% 39% 0.25x 99% 23% 0.5x 90% Not reported 1x (full trace) 49% Not reported Both protocols also worked on SGLang, LMDeploy, and TensorRT-LLM, in addition to vLLM. Step sizing also worked on multiple GPUs, including the A40, RTX 4090, RTX 5090, and H100. A reader trained on one GPU, though, didn’t recognize the signal on another; which step sizes give identical results depends on the GPU and software, so a reader trained on one setup doesn’t work on another. The main experiments ran on one Nvidia L40S . The consumer cards on the list mean this isn’t just something for the data center, and enthusiasts capable of training their own readers could play around with this themselves. In separate in-context games run by Africa on H200s, with no fine-tuning at all, the helper models used unmodified Qwen3-8B, a relatively small model without deeper refinement. Bob was an unmodified GLM model, which is larger, but ran at low effort. Pairing a small model with a larger one is common anyway, as in speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes tokens for a bigger one to check. What really mattered was how much Bob was told, as the table below shows. Unmodified GLM model reading the message board (chance is 12.5%) What else Bob was given Bob’s accuracy Cache explanation, baselines, direction of change 100% Same, without the direction 94% Cache explanation and a log of earlier rounds, no baselines 65% Log of earlier rounds only 66% Log only; Bob picks which mailboxes to check 17% (31% at high effort) Then again, this doesn’t say anything about what future models could achieve. Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, wrote the research’s code and figures, according to the authors, and Claude Opus 5.5, a frontier model, also “was able to arrive at” the protocols “with minimal prompting” after being told that engine step size affects kernel choice. Decoding accuracy also rose with model capability, which is the real concern. The researchers say the channels are “easy to close” and suggest three fixes: serve models on different engine instances, turn on batch-invariant kernels, which make activations bit-identical, and use per-user cache isolation. For the monitor, running it on a different engine instance than the policy “closes nearly every side channel.” vLLM already documents both fixes — cache salting and batch invariance — but they are opt-in. These fixes can reduce cache efficiency and performance, so they do come at a cost.

title: Denny’s touts renewed support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following reinstatement
summary: Denny's, the diner where Jensen Huang came up with the idea for Nvidia, has posted a 200-word statement to X in which it expressed its delight at his return to Nvidia after he initially resigned and admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
content: Following his recent resignation from the company and his return as CEO earlier this week, Jensen Huang has received a glowing statement of support from Denny's, the chain where he famously began his working life before founding Nvidia. The diner chain Denny's posted a 200-word statement to X in which it sought to maintain its links to the Nvidia founder, saying that there are "some things you just don’t take off the menu." Denny's, famously, is the diner where Huang came up with the idea for Nvidia before founding the then-GPU company, now an AI server outfit. Every story starts somewhere. We’re proud to be part of Jensen’s. https://t.co/WpWJdLFmIs November 25, 2026 Notably, the chain also noted that it has restored a plaque commemorating the occasion to "where it belongs," days after it was removed amid growing controversy over Huang and his affair with former Megaspeed employee Alice Huang. Megaspeed is now under criminal investigation over its involvement in bypassing U.S. export controls relating to Nvidia's advanced AI chips. It's also believed that Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, may also be a spy with connections to China's Ministry of State Security . Despite all of that, Denny's has very much hitched its trailer to Huang and his reputation, for better or worse. The diner's statement ends by reminding him that his booth "is always waiting and the coffee's on," although it's unclear whether he'll be able to make time for a visit between his upcoming visit to Congress to discuss the last few weeks' goings-on and joining board meetings with U.S. President Donald Trump . There is good news for Huang, though, even if he's found to have broken the law during his trysts with the suspected spy. Trump says that a pardon is "always an option," meaning Huang could be free to visit all the Denny's diners he wants to in the future. As for Nvidia, its share price has suffered the same fate as other tech stocks in recent weeks. It rallied after initially nosediving around the time of Huang's resignation, but has since continued its downward trajectory, having fallen almost 2.4 percentage points in the last five days and over 30 points in the last month.

title: Trump says a pardon for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is 'always an option'
summary: U.S. President Donald Trump says that he could pardon Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he finds himself in legal hot water over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang is set to meet with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next week.
content: U.S. President Donald Trump says that he could pardon returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he finds himself in legal hot water over his already-admitted affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed employee and an alleged Chinese spy . The Nvidia founder has since admitted to the company's board that he had more affairs than those already reported , including one with a direct report . Huang is set to meet with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next week and will be expected to answer questions about the affair, its effect on Nvidia, and how it impacts the national security of the country as a whole. Trump pushed for Huang's reinstatement, going so far as to pressure the Nvidia board via a telephone call. With that in mind, a NY Post report that he could consider pardoning Huang may not be all that surprising. Discussing Huang's meeting on December 1, Trump argued that the two-time Nvidia CEO doesn't need to worry about pleading the Fifth Amendment to avoid incriminating himself. Instead, Trump says, the whole saga is "an interesting story for people,” suggesting that perhaps the American people will learn more in the future. “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know, a very smart person,” Trump said of the man whose mistress is also married to an alleged Chinese spy herself. U.S. intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang passed information about Nvidia to Chinese officials during her affair with Jensen Huang (no relation). The good news, it seems, is that Trump is of the understanding that Alice Huang is the only woman Jensen was having an affair with who also has links to China's Ministry of State Security. When pushed on the potential for a pardon for Huang if he was found to have broken any laws, Trump admitted that “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.” The news will no doubt be music to the ears of Huang, with lawmakers expected to give him a grilling and some already not expecting him to be forthcoming in terms of the answers he offers to their questions. Nvidia's top lawyer will also have to answer questions about the company's position in all of this, although that'll come a day later, on December 2.

title: Two Californian Nvidia AI chip customers are really Chinese-owned
summary: Nvidia sells its advanced AI chips to two Californian companies with links to Chinese parent companies, including one that has already been blacklisted. Nvidia is only allowed to sell to specific companies, with export controls intended to prevent these chips from falling into the wrong hands in China.
content: While Nvidia is only allowed to sell its most advanced AI chips to whitelisted companies, it appears that two of its Californian customers are actually fronts for Chinese companies. Further, one of the Californian companies was renamed after its Chinese parent company was blacklisted, CBS News reports . The other one, which is on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners," is owned by a Chinese firm whose CEO graduated from a Chinese military university. It's reported that U.S.-based, Chinese-owned companies have been used as a way to work around export controls designed to prevent Nvidia's chips from being sold wholesale to China. Chips are routinely sold to companies in the U.S. before being leased or shipped to other companies in Southeast Asia. While Nvidia isn't allowed to sell its most capable AI chips to China, it can still do business with the country. It can sell graphics cards for use in personal gaming PCs as well as AI chips that don't use the company's latest, most capable technologies. But that hasn't stopped those chips from turning up in the most unlikely of places. Illegal Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs have been spotted in use inside China Telecom's network , and last year alone, it's believed that around $1 billion worth of Nvidia chips were smuggled into China. Earlier this year, nine people were indicted over the illegal export of Nvidia GPUs , while even older Nvidia hardware has seen huge price increases due to the unavailability of newer hardware. Megaspeed is one company that is accused of facilitating the breaking of export controls. The company is under criminal investigation currently , and it was recently blacklisted as a result . The company also happens to be a former employer of Alice Huang, the woman whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with when he resigned from the company earlier this month. Alice Huang is also believed to be a Chinese Spy , while her husband has even closer connections to a Chinese spy agency . Back in the U.S., RiCloud AI is an Nvidia customer owned by Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited, an outfit with headquarters in Shenzhen, China. Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, reportedly has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university operated by the Chinese military. Among RiCloud AI's customers is Agencia Comercial Spirits, a small whisky importer that pivoted to AI in 2025. Since then, it has committed to AI data center deals worth up to $598 million. Airvres is currently listed as an "elite" partner on Nvidia's website, yet it was previously called Inspur, the same name used by its Chinese parent company. The name change came after Inspur-related firms were added to a federal blocklist in March 2023. Airvres reportedly exported at least $5.6 billion of chips to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, including Nvidia's top-of-the-line Blackwell silicon. The chips went to two companies in Malaysia, one of which was Alice Huang's Megaspeed.

title: US defense officials considered using Cold War law to force Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO following his resignation, report claims
summary: Pentagon leaders considered using the Cold War-era Defense Production Act to pressure Nvidia to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as CEO following his resignation over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, with
content: Following the resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, U.S. defense leaders considered invoking a Cold War-era law in an attempt to force the company to reinstate him, according to a new report. Huang was given his CEO job back earlier this week, with the board reminding the founder of the importance of "candor and honesty" in the future. Now, The Washington Post reports that U.S. officials were so keen to ensure that Huang was reinstated that they brainstormed ideas as to how they could make it happen. One of the options on the table was the Defense Production Act, or DFA, a 1950 law that allows presidents to interfere with private companies. The law is usually used to force those companies to supply the military during wartime, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, wondered whether it could also be used to put pressure on Nvidia's board. While the DFA doesn't explicitly give the president the power to place a particular person into the CEO role at a company, it could still be wielded to achieve the same result. “Essentially, they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” one of three people reportedly familiar with the discussions said. Such a move would have limited Nvidia's ability to sell components for a profit, affecting its production plans and share price as a result. The way in which U.S. officials pushed for Huang's return before his November 23 reinstatement is unprecedented. Current U.S. President Donald Trump called for Huang to be given his job back on multiple occasions, including when talking to reporters at the White House . Trump also confirmed that he called into an Nvidia board meeting to pressure members to bring Huang back just 11 days after he resigned. And with Huang still set to face questions from China congressional and Senate Banking committees , Trump has admitted that a pardon for the CEO is "always an option." This came after it was suggested that Huang could plead the Fifth Amendment for fear of incriminating himself and landing himself in legal hot water. The U.S. military views Nvidia and its advanced AI chips as vital to national security, perhaps explaining why officials have been so keen to ensure Huang's return. Trump and Huang have a strong relationship, with the former joining the president aboard Air Force One for a recent trip to China. This came after Huang was initially snubbed for a trip that also included former Apple CEO Tim Cook and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

title: Credit rating agency puts Nvidia on notice for possible downgrade
summary: S&P Global Ratings says that it could lower Nvidia's credit rating because of various risks that it faces, including the smuggling allegations and the fact the lack of succession planning for its CEO.
content: S&P Global Ratings, one of the world’s largest rating agencies, announced that it’s putting Nvidia’s credit rating on watch as the company faces a possible downgrade. The agency says that the issues surrounding Jensen Huang regarding export control violations, as well as his resignation and subsequent reinstatement 11 days later, reveal the weakness of Nvidia’s management team and board oversight. “We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence,” the rating agency said in its press release. It also added, “Issues related to Nvidia’s China exposure also raise questions regarding geopolitical risk management and internal controls. While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the ‘key man’ risk to the forefront. The departure, then reinstatement of the CEO, does not sufficiently answer our questions regarding board oversight of executive code of conduct.” Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigned from the job on November 12, after multiple allegations of affairs, especially with Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, who’s also accused of enabling the smuggling of $7.5 billion worth of AI GPUs into China. Even though Huang left the company he founded in disgrace , he was reinstated to the position by the Nvidia board on November 23. This was a major surprise, especially as it had previously refused to bring him back due to the ongoing national security investigation into Jensen. However, it seems that Nvidia’s board of directors has folded to the pressure, especially after President Donald Trump himself said that he talked to them directly , with the board saying that it “received input from senior levels of the United States” that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Despite those assurances, the Nvidia chief still faces multiple investigations , including an internal inquiry at Nvidia, a private meeting with the House of Representatives’ Select Committee on China, and a public testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee, among others. Even though the AI chipmaker’s risk profile remains unchanged, S&P Global Ratings’ warning is a sign that the market is uneasy about the situation regarding stricter export controls and the allegations of chip diversion. The ratings agency said that the downgrade could happen in the next 90 days after it concludes its due diligence, although it expects any potential drop to “be limited to one notch, unless investigations or disclosures lead us to believe Nvidia’s reputation or future business prospects have been harmed.”

title: Ukraine downs Russian jet-drone with cheap high-powered laser for the first time
summary: Ukraine has shot down a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone using an air defense laser for the first time.
content: Ukraine has shot down a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone using an air defense laser, reports the Kyiv Independent . This is a first for the 'Blysk' laser system, developed by Ukraine's defense tech company Carmine Sky, and which was deployed on November 19. The news was supported by a Telegram post with embedded video shared by Serhii 'Flash' Beskrestnov, the defense tech advisor to President Zelensky. For the first time, Ukrainian forces have shot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone using a laser weapons system. https://t.co/PV9xTu3pdk November 25, 2026 Flash explains that the Blysk is currently being tested in active duty to protect an unnamed "critical infrastructure facility" [machine translation of Telegram post content]. Though only in testing for a few days, it seems to have already been a success, as it is the first time a laser has been used to destroy one of the speedy new jet-powered drones Russia has begun to deploy in the conflict. The 'Geran' drones mentioned by the source publication are Russian adaptations of the Iranian Shahed drones. Russia has used multiple iterations of the Iranian design, dubbed the Geran-2, Geran-5, etc. Despite the celebratory post highlighting the first jet drone laser kill, Flash was realistic about the technology's potentially slow rollout. "It is still too early to discuss serial production of the laser," wrote the tech advisor on Telegram. It isn't only Carmine Sky that is working on laser defense tech, noted Flash. This highly complex and capital-intensive battlefield tech is being worked upon by "several companies in Ukraine," it was claimed. We've also seen lasers touted as attractive anti-drone solutions by other nations. Even if they might be expensive to develop, lasers are often praised for their low cost per shot. Blysk reportedly has a power output of 4kW, and using a shot of energy of this magnitude is far cheaper than firing a missile, for example. We've seen it claimed that the UK's DragonFire laser weapon costs roughly £10 ($13) per shot in energy consumption, and the Blysk cost per shot is probably in the same ballpark. The source report says that weather hasn't been ideal for laser defenses recently, with "persistent cloud cover and fog." Unlike missiles and bullets, common weather phenomena like cloud cover can seriously weaken a laser beam before it reaches its target. Lasers will likely therefore never replace kinetic forms of air defense, but will be deployed to augment existing protections.

title: Exploring the Indium phosphide supply chain — the material constraint tightening the optical interconnect bottleneck
summary: The AI industry's shift to optical interconnects is overwhelming the concentrated InP supply chain behind lasers, transceivers, and co-packaged optics.
content: Indium phosphide (InP) is a compound material used in specialized chip-making. Unlike silicon, which is the fundamental building block for mainstream logic and memory chips, InP — made from indium and phosphorus — is mainly used to manufacture highly specialized photonic and high-frequency electronic chips, largely due to its outstanding optical properties. Its immensely expensive and complex manufacturing process also makes it impractical for the large volumes and die sizes needed for logic and memory chips. With the industry predicting a shortfall of this crucial material right as the shift to optical interconnects in data centers begins, we explore the current state of the supply chain. InP chips have powered high-speed lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and various other optical components used across the telecommunications industry and defense for decades. While the InP supply chain was relatively small and highly specialized, it was generally stable and sufficient to meet global demands. Then came the AI boom. As AI clusters hit the physical limits of moving enormous amounts of data over copper, the industry began the switch to optical interconnects. First came ever-faster optical transceivers. Now the industry is transitioning to silicon photonics , near-packaged optics, and co-packaged optics, bringing optical links progressively closer to the processors themselves. InP is central to much of this transition, building the critical active optical components needed to turn electrical data into light and back again. Individual AI data centers are already being built around hundreds of thousands of accelerators, with upcoming gigawatt-scale buildouts expected to house millions . Connecting those processors translates into demand for millions upon millions of indispensable optical components, all relying on the same relatively tiny InP supply chain. Japan's Sumitomo Electric and U.S.-headquartered AXT together account for almost 80% of global InP substrate manufacturing, with JX Advanced Metals adding roughly another 10%. AXT, however, manufactures most of its InP substrates in China, where exports now require government licenses, further exacerbating the situation. It gets worse: China accounts for around 70% of global refined indium output, which is recovered as a byproduct of processing zinc. Export controls mean that restrictions apply to both the material itself and the finished wafer. The resulting squeeze is already sending ripples across the industry, with several companies predicting shortfalls. Michael Hurlston, CEO of optical-component manufacturer Lumentum, said in July that the company's InP fabs were shipping more than 30% below customer demand , despite rapid capacity expansion. Coherent also described InP capacity as the “primary constraint” on its transceiver business. A simple solution would be to expand the supply chain. However, growing large, low-defect InP crystals is difficult, while qualifying new suppliers requires time that doesn't align with the industry's demand. Furthermore, expanding substrate and laser-fabrication capacity can take years. Meanwhile, to secure optical components capacity for its accelerators, Nvidia has invested $2 billion each in Lumentum and Coherent , attaching multibillion-dollar purchase commitments and future capacity rights to both deals. Both companies, along with several others in the supply chain, are frantically pursuing solutions. What is indium phosphide? Indium phosphide belongs to the III-V family of compound semiconductors, named after the periodic-table groups of their constituent elements; in InP’s case, indium and phosphorus. Its better-known relatives include gallium arsenide and gallium nitride. Indium phosphide’s distinguishing property, which separates it from silicon, is its direct bandgap, measured at about 1.34 eV at room temperature. In a direct-bandgap material, electrons dropping across the gap release their energy efficiently as photons, making the material particularly useful for lasers and other active optical devices. Silicon, on the other hand, has an indirect bandgap, meaning that the same transition requires an additional interaction with a crystal lattice and mostly sheds its energy as heat instead. Therefore, while the material can — in silicon photonics — guide, split, and modulate light using structures fabricated with mature CMOS processes, it does not produce the light beam. As a result, Modern silicon-photonics systems commonly rely on a III-V laser source, most commonly based on the InP material system, to provide the light that the silicon circuitry manipulates. (Image credit: Shutterstock) The fiber-optic wavelength window’s alignment with InP's properties is another reason for the material's ubiquity. Modern telecom and data-center links commonly operate around 1,310 nm and 1,550 nm, where optical fiber exhibits favorable transmission characteristics. Pure InP itself does not emit at those exact wavelengths. However, InGaAsP and InAlGaAs alloys, which are grown on lattice-matched InP substrates, can have their bandgaps engineered for those bands. InGaAs layers on InP are also highly effective photodetectors at telecom wavelengths. These characteristics and functionalities make the InP platform critical to many active functions in optical communications, including distributed-feedback (DFB) lasers, electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs), continuous-wave (CW) lasers, semiconductor optical amplifiers, photodetectors, and complete photonic integrated circuits. Silicon photonics and InP consequently complement each other. Silicon provides scalable optical circuitry, while InP provides efficient light generation and several high-performance active optical devices. Beyond photonics, InP is also commonly used in high-frequency electronic chips. Electrons move through the material far faster than through silicon, giving it strong high-frequency performance that makes it suitable for millimeter-wave and terahertz electronics, radar receivers, and high-speed data converters. This market is much smaller than photonics, but it has few substitutes at the top of the frequency range. Indium phosphide’s roles across telecommunications and AI data centers InP lasers and transceivers have been converting electrical signals into light for long-haul fiber networks, metro links, submarine cables, and eventually shorter-reach data-center connections for decades. Despite 5G rollouts driving demand higher, the indium phosphide supply chain remained a stable, moderately sized business with predictable growth. The AI boom has now driven demand up by several orders of magnitude. Modern AI clusters can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnected accelerators that continuously exchange data. Copper remains a cheap, effective connector over short distances, but electrical losses, signal integrity, and power requirements progressively worsen as bandwidth and distance increase. This has led to the rapid adoption of optical interconnects . In this setup, a modulator encodes electrical data from the switch or accelerator onto light from a laser. Fiber cables then carry it across the link to a photodetector that converts the received photons back into an electrical signal. In pluggable transceivers, many of these functions are integrated into a compact module plugged into the front of a network switch, with InP-based components executing several steps in the process. Lumentum's 200G EML, for example, monolithically combines a wavelength-locked DFB laser and an electro-absorption modulator on its InP platform, and is designed for 200-Gbps-per-lane links used in 1.6T transceivers. Coherent is producing InP EMLs, high-power CW lasers, and high-speed photodiodes for the same generation of hardware. As aggregate link speeds move from 400G and 800G to 1.6T and beyond, the number and performance of these InP-based optical components become increasingly important. Quantum-X InfiniBand Photonics Switch (Image credit: Getty Images / Bloomberg) At the same time, the industry is bringing optics right to the board with co-packaged optics (CPO) to further shorten the distance data travels. Conventional pluggable optics leave around 15 to 30 centimeters (5.90 to 11.81 inches) of high-speed copper trace between the switch ASIC and the optical module. CPO brings the optical engine onto the accelerator package as a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) chip, shrinking that electrical path and reducing power consumption. Nvidia's Quantum-X and Spectrum-X photonics switches are among the first major AI platforms built around that approach. While they integrate several optical functions onto the boards, PIC chips do not generate the laser. CPO and silicon-photonics designs still mostly use external InP CW lasers to supply light to the silicon photonic circuits, further consolidating the demand for indium phosphide in AI data centers and the industry as a whole. The state of the supply chain As a result of the enormous, rapidly expanding market for the material, indium phosphide’s supply chain is constrained at several points, starting with the raw material itself. Unlike many metals which are mined from dedicated deposits, indium is typically recovered as a trace byproduct of processing zinc sulfide ore. Manufacturers then combine high-purity indium and phosphorus and grow them into a single-crystal InP ingot, or boule, which they process into substrate wafers with tightly controlled properties. Next, manufacturers grow extremely thin epitaxial layers of InP-related compounds over it, commonly using metal-organic chemical vapor deposition. The epiwafer then goes through several chip-making processes and module assembly to become optical chips and devices. Indium production's dependence on Zinc processing creates bottlenecks in InP's supply chain, right at the beginning of the stream. The USGS put global primary refined indium production at roughly 1,100 tonnes in 2025, with China accounting for 760 tonnes. For context, the BBC estimates that 30,000 tonnes of electronic-grade silicon used exclusively to make microchips are mined yearly. The United States imports all of the InP it consumes, producing nothing. Meanwhile, indium substrate manufacturers Japan's Sumitomo and JX Metals source more than 90% of their high-purity indium feedstock from China, meaning even non-Chinese substrate makers begin their process with Chinese material. Further downstream, at the substrate manufacturing level, Sumitomo Electric holds roughly 40% of the global InP substrate market, U.S.-based AXT around 35%, and JX Advanced Metals about 10%. Together, the three control more than 90% of capacity. Although AXT is headquartered in California, most of its InP substrate production runs through its Beijing Tongmei subsidiary, which puts it directly under China's export licensing regime. Other fringe substrate manufacturers include Freiberger Compound Materials in Germany and a growing set of Chinese entrants, including Yunnan Germanium. The supply chain is also highly concentrated at the device and component level, with Coherent and Lumentum dominating Western laser and component production. IQE supplies epitaxial wafers, and Japanese firms, including Mitsubishi Electric, supply laser components. Chinese module makers such as Innolight and Eoptolink assemble a large share of the world's finished 800G modules, pairing Western lasers with Broadcom and Marvell DSPs. We recently explored how this entanglement complicates any attempt to decouple the two ecosystems, even as the FCC is considering a ban on Chinese optical hardware . Coherent primarily sources substrates from AXT, while Lumentum relies heavily on Sumitomo and JX. On the technical side, wafer-size limitations in InP semiconductors add another constraint. While silicon logic and memory moved to 300-mm wafers in the early 2000s, the InP industry is only now transitioning from 3-inch to 6-inch (150-mm) production; primarily because the material is brittle, expensive, and grown in small boules, factors that limit wafer size. Doubling the wafer diameter gives four times the area. Coherent's six-inch line, for example, yields more than four times as many devices as its three-inch line at a lower cost per die. On the other hand, moving a fab to six-inch requires new crystal-growth recipes, new handling equipment, new process qualification, and extensive customer requalification. The supply chain was already struggling under these constraints when, in February 2025, Beijing placed InP, trimethylindium, triethylindium, and the technology used to produce them under export controls , requiring licenses for overseas shipments. AXT called the export controls its most significant current challenge, noting that even with sufficient capacity and strong demand, its ability to ship outside China depends on Chinese licensing decisions. The shortfall and the race to expand The widening gap between demand and InP industry output points to a fast-approaching shortfall. Coherent first warned of an InP shortage on its May earnings call. At the close of its fiscal year in August, CEO Jim Anderson described indium phosphide availability as the company's primary constraint, confirming that transceiver assembly and test capacity were available. Lumentum CEO Hurlston said in July that telecom customers historically ordered lasers in the hundreds, while Nvidia and the hyperscalers were asking for hundreds of millions. Despite operating multiple InP fabs, Lumentum was shipping more than 30% below customer requirements. Earlier in the year, Hurlston said the company's capacity was sold out through 2027 and probably into 2028, even with the expanded output. In both cases, capacity was mostly bought out via Nvidia’s $4 billion investment. To ease the multifaceted bottleneck, the industry is pursuing several solutions simultaneously, primarily expansions. Coherent is expanding its Sherman, Texas campus, reportedly described as the first and largest high-volume 6-inch InP semiconductor manufacturing facility. Washington signed a letter of intent in June for up to $50 million in CHIPS Act funding for the expansion. Coherent is now on track to double internal InP output in 2026, one quarter ahead of its original plan, and more than double it again by the end of 2027, while also adding 6-inch production in Sweden and Zurich. Lumentum, meanwhile, is converting a 240,000-square-foot former Qorvo gallium-arsenide facility in North Carolina, which it bought for about $18 million, into another InP fab. The relevance of these expansions largely depends on the downstream InP substrate supply. Lumentum signed an agreement in July to reserve AXT InP substrate capacity through 2031, with an initial $43.5 million deposit and another $43.5 million payment contemplated for 2028. Coherent signed its own three-year 6-inch supply agreement with AXT a month earlier and prepaid $22.3 million against committed capacity. The substrate suppliers are also expanding in kind. AXT is channeling fresh funds into Beijing Tongmei to double capacity by the end of 2026 and double it again in 2027. Similarly, JX Advanced Metals plans to invest roughly ¥120 billion ($746 million) through FY2030 to lift capacity seven to ten times above FY2025 levels, its largest-ever commitment in semiconductor materials. Indium production — the uppermost stage of the stream — is far less active, with the biggest hurdle being the reliance on Zinc production. Global zinc mine production hasn't grown materially since 2011, sitting at or below 13 million tonnes a year, according to analysts. Wood Mackenzie expects just 0.1% growth in 2026. On the other hand, not everyone expects the crunch to last. LightCounting estimated in April that optical component demand exceeded supply by about 30% but projected that shortages would largely clear by the end of 2026 as new capacity comes online. There are also viable, albeit slow, technical workarounds to ease the crunch. Heterogeneous integration bonds InP onto silicon to combine the strengths of both, while quantum dot lasers offer better temperature stability for uncooled operation. Furthermore, researchers continue to push InP quantum dot structures grown directly on silicon substrates. While these do not remove indium from the equation, they change how much each device needs and how it attaches, reducing consumption. Photonics is widely viewed as one of AI's major bottlenecks. However, the indium phosphide supply chain is itself tightening that bottleneck.

title: Nvidia stops AI GPU shipments to Southeast Asia amid purported China cloud access ban, report claims
summary: Data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia are now required to obtain export licenses if they want to get their Nvidia AI GPUs delivered.
content: AI data centers in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia are facing trouble as Nvidia has reportedly ordered its manufacturing partners to stop shipping AI servers to the region. According to the Financial Times, Dell, Supermicro, and other firms that make AI servers using Nvidia AI GPUs have told their customers from the four countries that the AI chip maker has forbidden them to ship their orders. The move comes as the U.S. closed the loophole that let Chinese AI companies rent compute from data centers outside China equipped with advanced AI chips sourced from American semiconductor manufacturers like Nvidia. The U.S. has banned the export of advanced AI chips to China since 2022 in an effort to limit its advancement. Even though President Trump eventually allowed Nvidia to export H100 AI GPUs to China in December 2025, companies that wanted to buy them needed to secure an import license from the Commerce Department. Aside from that, the White House is also collecting a 25% fee for every chip, making it more expensive for a data center in China to buy them. Because of this, many Chinese AI labs are instead renting compute from data centers located abroad. They mostly do this in Southeast Asia, which is just around a four-to-six-hour flight from major cities like Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Shanghai, although some firms are looking in further areas like Europe . It remains unclear if Nvidia’s order is permanent or temporary, but the new export rules give cloud providers 90 days to apply for an export license and prove that their customers do not include restricted entities. However, one cloud provider executive told the Financial Times that there are no clear instructions on how to go about this. “There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” they said. “No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.” This sudden halt of orders is causing trouble for many data centers in Southeast Asia. Sources say that Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud company with a deal to provide compute to ByteDance, is losing financing for the project as bankers have stopped issuing credit to the tune of $500 million as Nvidia GPU shipments to the region remain in jeopardy. The Chinese social media giant could also potentially drop out of the arrangement, as it won’t be able to access the powerful Nvidia chips that many AI labs still prefer for training their models.

title: TSMC’s $22.6 billion Texas plan wouldn’t make 2nm-or-better chips until 2031
summary: TSMC’s Texas filing describes a $22.6 billion project in Brazos County for 2nm or more advanced chips, starting production in 2031.
content: TSMC has made an application for a new fab and campus near College Station, Brazos County, Texas. The proposed fab would be just one county over from Terafab, would likely share supply chains, and would be positioned to make 2nm-class chips by 2031, with the $22.6 billion plan detailing how the Taiwanese chipmaker is planning to expand its U.S. operations. An application under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program for a school property-tax limit shows TSMC is weighing a new fab site. The fab wouldn’t make 2nm or more advanced chips until 2031, six years after 2nm volume production began in Taiwan. It would come with a school-tax break valued at around $354 million. This would be the company’s “second campus” for advanced chipmaking in the U.S. and the first outside Arizona. The Comptroller has recommended the tax application for approval, which the school district and the governor still have to grant. The application comes from TSMC Arizona Corporation, which is TSMC’s subsidiary located in Phoenix. Construction is projected to start in 2027, but the plan remains under evaluation, and nothing in the filing commits TSMC to buy the land or to build on it. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) TSMC is looking to build out more in the U.S. because most of its large customers are based there and the government has been “very helpful” in pursuing additional fab capacity, Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said in October. Texas is one option for expanding beyond Arizona, though the filing doesn’t say what drew TSMC there. TSMC judges each site on its tax environment, workforce availability, utility capacity and cost, and site and infrastructure readiness, as well as its “long-term scalability and expansion potential.” TSMC says Arizona offers “established operational efficiencies and lower capital risk,” and that the tax incentive would aid this further. T SMC has “nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress,” Wei said on the October earnings call, including 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan and “another five to six fabs overseas.” Annual capacity for its 2nm (N2) family is expected to more than double in 2027. TSMC also expects more of its fabs to be ramping up in the U.S. Texas wouldn’t begin commercial operations until 2031, and the economic model filed with the plan doesn’t have it at full operations until 2032. By contrast, the second fab in Arizona is expected to begin volume production in Q3 2027, but at 3nm. In Taiwan, N2 has been in high-volume production since Q4 2025. TSMC expects A14, its next full node after N2, to enter risk production in 2027 and volume in 2028 . By 2031, A14 is set to have been in volume production for about three years, so a Texas fab that starts on 2nm would be at least a generation behind TSMC’s leading edge. Taiwan has also debated limits on how advanced TSMC’s overseas fabs can be . TSMC’s roadmap and the Texas timeline Milestone Where When 2nm (N2) volume production Taiwan Q4 2025 A16 (a 2nm-family node) volume production TSMC, site not stated 2027 (expected) 3nm volume production, second fab Arizona Q3 2027 A14 volume production TSMC, site not stated 2028 High-NA EUV adoption TSMC, site not stated 2030 (planned) 2nm “and/or more advanced,” commercial operations Texas (proposed) 2031 The new site would have one or more fabs but, as it stands, Brazos County’s announcement describes one. For scale, we’ve estimated that a single 2nm-class module with about 20,000 wafer starts a month costs $25 billion to $35 billion, so this plan’s $22.6 billion budget falls below the low end of that range. The price tag is split in multiple ways, with $8.60 billion for buildings and other real property, while 62% of the total, or $14.02 billion, is for tooling, machinery and equipment, a category that on the filing’s list also covers power, HVAC, cleanroom, water and gas systems. The building's spending would come first, in 2027, 2028, and 2029 alone. Tool spending would begin in that last year and peak at $9.05 billion in 2030, with about 65% of the tool budget landing in that year, before ending at $963.9 million in 2032 — the form’s Schedule A stops at 2031 and $21.66 billion total. TSMC’s proposed Texas project: spending and hiring by year Year Buildings Machinery and equipment New hires 2027 $729.0 million — 0 2028 $2.59 billion — 757 2029 $5.28 billion $649.2 million 1,110 2030 — $9.05 billion 232 2031 — $3.36 billion 0 2032 — $963.9 million 0 Total $8.60 billion $14.02 billion 2,099 The tool spending schedule lines up with a change in how TSMC prints its chips. Lithography, the step in the chipmaking process that uses light to project circuit patterns onto the wafer, requires advanced machines. The most advanced do it with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light. High-NA EUV tools have a higher numerical aperture, gathering more light to print finer features in one pass. Wei said TSMC intends to use High-NA in 2030 , which matches the 2030 peak in Texas tool spending, but that is a company-wide plan, and nothing in the Texas plan gives a delivery schedule or names High-NA tools specifically. What the plan does spell out is its list of eligible property: fab and central utility plant buildings, cleanroom systems, ultra-pure water and wastewater treatment with water-reclaim systems, bulk and specialty gas as well as automated material handling, and gas-insulated switchgear. Also named is mask or reticle shop equipment as well as lithography, etch, deposition, implant, chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), diffusion, and clean/wet tools, by type, although the list names no tool vendors, EUV counts, or wafer capacity. The mask shop is highlighted as “co-located within the fab and integral to the manufacturing process.” Masks are patterned plates used by a lithography tool to project their patterns onto each wafer, one per chip layer, and every new design needs its own set. Making them on site suggests the fab is meant to stand on its own. Wei also said TSMC is working with ASML on a 12-inch photomask by 2031, which is the year the Texas site would open. The plan’s location is in Brazos County, Texas, sited across 86 parcels and almost 3,232 acres of land, which is about five square miles. This compares to TSMC’s Phoenix campus at about 1,078 acres on the county tax roll, with about 902 more purchased in January; this leaves the Texas site at about 1.6 times that total. TSMC would build and manage the site, which sets it apart from Terafab, a fab a TSMC customer is planning one county over: Wei has confirmed talks about using its capacity but said any such fab would have to be run by TSMC. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Residents in development areas for fabs and data centers tend to raise two concerns, and both are related to utility usage. The first is power: a local report says Bryan Texas Utilities provides that for the proposed area, but it’s unclear who would serve the fab. For scale, a utility filing in Arizona reportedly puts TSMC’s built-out Phoenix campus at about 1.9 gigawatts, a figure for the whole campus, not a single fab. The second is water: Wellborn Special Utility District reportedly provides service, while the developer is said to intend to buy its water from a third party instead. As a comparison, a state document on an unnamed company’s $45 billion, two-fab project in Sherman, as reported by the Dallas Business Journal , lists 8 to 10 million gallons a day to start with a peak at 20 to 25 million after buildout, but this isn’t a 1:1. That project is targeting production in Q4 2029. Economic impacts are a significant part of the deal: the plan projects 2,099 direct jobs by 2030, while the agreement would require only 35, the legal minimum. Pay, on the other hand, comes with a projected average salary nearly double the wage level that would need clearing. Texas appears willing to work with TSMC on this, with a recommendation for approval signed by Deputy Comptroller Noah Betz this week. The gross tax benefit would build over 14 years, starting four years before the formal incentive period, and would cut the district’s maintenance and operations (M&O) levy on the project nearly in half. Even so, the full $354.1 million is only 1.6% of the $22.6 billion investment. In return, TSMC would have to post a performance bond equal to 10% of the benefit. The Comptroller believes the incentive is a compelling factor — TSMC would not invest in Texas without it — but the office says it has not audited or verified the company’s projections. TSMC, for its part, calls the limit “determinative.” The Texas tax deal in numbers Measure Figure Source Direct jobs TSMC projects 2,099 by 2030 Application Jobs the agreement would require 35 Comptroller Average salary TSMC projects $135,687 in 2028, rising 2% a year Application Minimum average wage for the project’s jobs $73,603 Comptroller Construction workers, 2027–2029 9,841 a year on average; 18,134 at the 2029 peak Consultant’s model Out-of-town visitors 708 a year; average stay 41 days Consultant’s model Tax benefit, total $354.1 million Comptroller Tax benefit during construction, 2028–2031 $123.6 million Comptroller Tax benefit in the incentive period, 2032–2041 $230.6 million Comptroller School M&O tax over 20 years, without the agreement $759.3 million Comptroller School M&O tax over 20 years, with the agreement $405.2 million Comptroller Performance bond $35.4 million Comptroller A potentially far larger incentive is federal: a tax credit worth 35 cents back to every qualifying dollar spent , as long as construction technically begins before the end of the year. “Qualified” means the cost of the fab’s depreciable physical property that is integral to running the fab, meaning the buildings and the tools, in the year each goes into service, and “construction” means actual physical work of a significant nature or paying or incurring at least 5% of the qualifying property’s cost, with work continuing afterward. Construction here is projected to start in 2027, after that cutoff, though off-site work under a binding written contract or early spending this year could still count, and an extension has been proposed in the Senate. The land doesn’t count in this equation, and neither does office space. This is also a credit off the tax bill, dollar for dollar, not a deduction. The rate was 25% under the 2022 CHIPS Act and rose to 35% for property placed in service after 2025. If the full $22.6 billion qualified, that would be about $7.9 billion back, but not every dollar qualifies. If Texas doesn’t work out, TSMC is also considering “a new land parcel in Arizona,” which would be closer to the existing North Phoenix site. TSMC says that may make many things easier, such as handling a workforce and the logistics, with the ability to use existing suppliers and relationships on known infrastructure. This is an incentive for the state of Texas to give the tax break. The tax agreement needs approval from both the College Station ISD board and the governor. The district also owns one of the parcels on TSMC’s list for the site: almost 91 acres, with a 24,496-square-foot building from 2024. The board has set a public hearing for Dec. 10, with public comment, and could approve the project’s reinvestment zone that day. The district has 30 days from the day it receives the application, which puts its deadline in late December. As for Brazos County, town halls could reportedly begin as early as the first week of December, though the county has promised only one, “in the near future.” Assuming things move forward, the real measure begins with the first phase on land. Even if production arrives a generation late, it would be a positive development for U.S.-based chipmaking.

title: TSMC's A14 1.4nm-class node is ready for chip design
summary: TSMC announces availability of its version 0.9 process design kit for its A14 manufacturing technology. Availability of the v0.9 version of PDK signals that the fabrication process is generally ready for design and production.
content: TSMC announced at its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop this week that its A14 (1.4nm-class) fabrication technology is ready for customer design work and version 0.9 of its process design kit (PDK) is ready. TSMC also detailed Boost Cells, a way for the new node to deliver 14% higher performance compared to N2P, and how customers can migrate their designs to A13 in the future. Furthermore, Cadence and Synopsys have both completed full design-flow certification on an Arm Cortex-A725 CPU core, which gives chip designers two validated toolchains to build their 14A chips. "A14 0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design in," a TSMC spokesman said on stage at the 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop. Boost Cells and Low-Power Cells provide further improvements A14 uses TSMC's 2 nd Generation nanosheet transistors and its NanoFlex Pro standard cell architecture, which supports Boost Cells to enable higher performance as well as Low-Power Cells to reduce power consumption. Designers can place compact high-speed Boost Cells on critical paths (which resembles Intel's Turbo Cells supported by its 14A fabrication technology) and use Low-Power Cells with narrower nanosheets for general logic or parts of the chip that do not need high performance. In general, TSMC promises A14 with NanoFlex Pro optimizations to deliver a 14% speed gain at the same power or a 23% reduction in total power at the same speed compared to N2P with NanoFlex. In a separate comparison against baseline N2P, TSMC put A14 at 50% higher energy efficiency, 22% higher drawn transistor density, and 23% higher logic density. TSMC process comparison against baseline N2P Metric N2P N2P NanoFlex N2U NanoFlex Pro A14 NanoFlex Pro A13 NanoFlex Pro Energy efficiency Baseline +12% +23% +50% +58% Transistor density (drawn) Baseline +11% +16% +22% +22% Logic density (silicon) Baseline 0% +2% +23% +30% A14 also gives customers a path to A13. The foundry says customers can cut die area by about 6% without changes to their A14 design flow. Furthermore, to take even more advantage of A13 and get 5% higher energy efficiency, all the designers have to do is re-engineer the M0 metal layer, reshape OD, and use VT Flex cells (cells that can use different threshold-voltage options for their NMOS and PMOS transistors). TSMC expects to start risk production using A14 in the second half of 2027, with mass production following in the second half of 2028. Chief executive C.C. Wei said in October that the company had already seen more customer activity on A14 than on N2 at a comparable stage of development and expects A14 to become a bigger node than its 2nm-class predecessor. A13 is set to reach the high-volume manufacturing stage in the second half of 2029. A14 PDK and ecosystem nearly ready One of the key parts of the TSMC announcement is the readiness of the 0.9 version of the PDK and the electronic design automation (EDA) tools ecosystem. What matters about v0.9 is that the industry considers this revision ready for design work, which means that customers can start designing chips with confidence that they will meet their performance and power goals. Furthermore, TSMC has validated two complete flows — by Cadence and Synopsys for A14, with Siemens EDA's flow coming later. "Today, both Cadence and Synopsys have successfully completed full design flow certification for the Cortex-A725," the spokesman said. "This program tests the full chain of implementation and sign-off EDA tools with TSMC foundation IP. We expect it to benefit the entire A14 design community. This table summarizes A14 v0.9 certification for our three major EDA partners, Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens, across automatic placement and routing, library characterization, timing, power, EM/IR, and other sign-off flows. Siemens is targeting Q4 for transistor-level EM/IR certification. So the A14 v0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design-in. Cadence and Synopsys also had certified tools for automatic placement and routing, library characterization, timing and power analysis, custom circuit design, and electromigration and voltage-drop (EM/IR) analysis at both the design and transistor levels. Synopsys alone had certified transistor-level timing analysis, which gave it coverage across all 13 categories versus 12 for Cadence and five for Siemens EDA. Cadence and Synopsys also completed full-flow certification on an Arm Cortex-A725 design with TSMC foundation IP, from synthesis and physical implementation through electrical, physical, and thermal sign-off. Siemens EDA's transistor-level EM/IR certification is in progress and is due in Q4 2026.

title: Take-Two wipes out 3,007 GTA 6 PC port repos from GitHub in massive DMCA crackdown
summary: Despite Take-Two's effort to shut down projects to port GTA VI, multiple projects have reported progress and could now run the game at lower frame rates on PCs.
content: GTA VI is only currently available on the PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S, with no word yet on when a PC port will arrive. However, this has not stopped enterprising gamers and developers from working on their own PC version, especially with the release of the AI-powered Reverse Engineer Anything tool . Take-Two Interactive is not taking kindly to this, though, with VideoCardz reporting that the company has issued a DMCA takedown on 3,007 repositories on GitHub. This is the biggest action that Rockstar’s parent company has taken to protect GTA VI so far, which came just a day after a 15-year-old’s recompilation project was shut down on both Discord and GitHub. GTA 6 on pc now runs visually identical to the consoles Vlctory emulator have loaded the full shaders of GTA 6 on pc now https://t.co/QrgoeCQ0GD November 25, 2026 Despite the massive crackdown, it seems that development is simply moving away from the public platform into private spaces. PortWatch VI , a website tracking the work on unofficial GTA VI PC ports, is currently following 30 projects, with one of the more successful ones reportedly playing for over 90 minutes on an RTX 3050 GPU without any crashes, albeit at an unplayable 1 to 3 FPS. There’s also a post on the r/FitGirlRepack subreddit claiming that an unofficial port could already hit 30 FPS, with the developers working on it targeting 60 FPS within the next three days. They also expect to release the source code within the same time frame. Just crazy how far this is going from r/FitGirlRepack Porting games to other platforms used to be a difficult, time-intensive job, but the proliferation of AI tools has made it so much easier (although still requiring skill and effort). This is why one game decompilation hub froze its leaderboard , which had turned into a hollow numbers game as teams rushed to ship PC buggy or laggy PC ports. Anthropic has also taken steps to prevent Claude from being used for video game cloning and reverse-engineering , but independent developers could use other AI tools, like locally run open-weight models, to do the job for them. There have been rumors that Rockstar will launch the game on PC as early as the first quarter of 2027, a massive improvement over the 18-month delay PC gamers had to endure with the previous installment. Rockstar’s parent company certainly wants to recoup the over $2 billion spent on developing the game, and having it available to the millions of PC gamers would certainly help with that goal. But the power that AI has given to developers to allow them to make unofficial ports much more quickly than before is certainly adding to the pressure.

title: Solo developer vibe codes a gallery hosting 36 classic GPU demos
summary: A solo developer known as arkits has created an online gallery to view classic 3D graphics demos live in the browser.
content: Once upon a time, graphics chip vendors made small applications to demonstrate the power of their new hardware. The most accessible were those from 3dfx, ATI Technologies, NVIDIA, and Matrox, since these were the companies dominating PC graphics at the time. If you're nostalgic for that era, you've got to check out this GPU Demo Gallery , because the enterprising creator Archit 'arkits' Khode has ported 36 classic PC graphics card demos to the web, and you can view them right in your browser. The GPU Demo Gallery homepage. You can click through to each demo and view them live in your browser. (Image credit: arkits) It's hard to appreciate from a modern perspective, but in the early 1990s, high-end real-time 3D graphics were largely the domain of specialized workstations costing tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars. By the middle of the decade, companies like 3dfx, Rendition, and VideoLogic ( known for PowerVR ) were promising to bring hardware-accelerated 3D graphics with filtered textures to ordinary PCs at interactive frame rates for a few hundred bucks. It was honestly hard to believe. So what's the simplest way to prove your hardware can do what you say it can? Make a demo and actually show it running in person on your hardware. Developing a full game takes a tremendous amount of time, money, and expertise, but a focused tech demo can concentrate on a particular feature or rendering technique and show it off without needing all the systems that make a game playable. And so the GPU tech demo was born. The Radeon 9700 "Pipe Dream" demo was one of the most impressive things I'd ever seen on a PC in 2002. The song is great too! (Image credit: Animusic/AMD) "Demos" have a long culture going back way before the 3D accelerator. The "demo scene" (now often written as one word, 'demoscene' ) goes back to the mid 1980s, the Commodore 64 and the 16-bit micro era, particularly on the Amiga and Atari ST. There's not much of a direct cultural connection between the demoscene and commercial GPU tech demos, but there was some overlap in the talent involved; NVIDIA, for example, had demoscene veterans on its demo team, including programmer Hubert 'Sigfrid' Nguyen of Impact Studios. The demos in the gallery start from the earliest 3dfx Voodoo demos like 'Demoroom' and 'Flip' and go up through the NVIDIA 'Box of Smoke' demo meant to show off GPU-accelerated computational fluid dynamics. There are some other rough edges; the site has the unmistakable feel of a vibe-coded project, and some of the shortcomings show through in the demos themselves. The Toy Soldiers demo has various problems, including broken reflections and specularity as well as incorrect soldier behavior on Panic mode. The right side is the original demo. (Image credit: NVIDIA) The famous NVIDIA Wolfman demo for the GeForce 4 Ti cards lacks its fur (which was the point of the demo), the 3dfx Valley of Ra demo doesn't render correctly (and the controls don't work), and the Toy Soldiers demo is missing all specularity. Also, as Hacker News commenter Narishma points out, most of these demos should be compatible with WebGL1, yet they all require WebGL2 or WebGPU support. Beyond that, there are a number of key demos missing that I'd like to see added, although the owner of the site is working fast with the help of Claude. When I first checked the site yesterday afternoon, there were only 26 demos, and the most glaring omission was the famous NVIDIA 'Dawn' demo for the GeForce FX GPUs. The lovely sprite is there now, as is ATI's incredible 'Pipe Dream' demo for the R300 (Radeon 9700/9800) family. This demo, where the lightning lights the scene and throws spark particles, was very impressive in 2001. (Image credit: NVIDIA) Hopefully, arkits can get the errors in the demos cleaned up, and it would be cool to see some classic graphics demos from other vendors implemented. Personally, I'd love to see the DICE-created Matrox EMBM demo and the PowerVR Kyro Energy and Still Life demos, as well as the impressive Dolphins demo for the original Xbox. The early G-SYNC Pendulum and Freesync Windmill demos would be cool, too. Still, even in its current state, arkits' gallery is a wonderful preservation effort for a tiny world that only a handful of people even remember.
